notes: Slot 0 Rhodesian Front (Smith). Coalition slot 13 holds Government House (Dupont as Officer Administering the Government) since the RF governed alone. ZAPU (Soviet-backed) and ZANU (Chinese-backed) follow MD in slots 4/5 with MD sprites; ZANLA as separate Maoist army in 19. Centre Party in 2. Republic proclaimed 2 March 1970 is after start, so no date switch.

0.name: Rhodesian Front
0.text:
The Rhodesian Front was founded in 1962 by white settlers determined to block African majority rule. It swept the 1962 and 1965 elections and, under Prime Minister Ian Smith, issued the Unilateral Declaration of Independence in November 1965. On 1 January 1970 it rules alone, fresh from the 1969 referendum that approved a republican constitution entrenching white control.

The RF promises 'responsible government in responsible hands', defends the Land Tenure Act and fights the guerrilla incursions from Zambia. It casts itself as a bulwark of Western civilisation against communism, yet faces British and UN sanctions. Its strength lies in white farmers, artisans and civil servants, in tight control of the security forces, and in the lifelines running through South Africa and Portuguese Mozambique.

1.name: The Federal Old Guard
1.text:
The Federal Old Guard are the men who ran the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and the old United Federal Party before the Rhodesian Front swept them aside. Their figurehead is Sir Roy Welensky, the last federal prime minister, who lost his comeback bid in 1964 and now watches Smith's rebellion from Salisbury with open misgivings.

They stand for gradual 'partnership' between the races under a qualified franchise, a negotiated return to legality with Britain and an end to sanctions. Fiercely anti-communist and pro-Commonwealth, they draw on the business community, the Salisbury professional class and English-language newspapers. Their leverage lies in their links to London and the mining houses rather than in votes.

2.name: Centre Party
2.text:
The Centre Party was founded in 1968 by moderate whites and Africans who opposed the drift toward a racially entrenched republic. Led by the farmer Pat Bashford, it campaigned against the 1969 constitutional proposals and is preparing to contest both the white roll and the African seats in the first republican election.

It calls for a non-racial qualified franchise, a settlement with Britain and the gradual repeal of land segregation. Firmly anti-communist and pro-Western, it appeals to liberal professionals, churchmen, some businessmen and educated Africans. Its weakness is a narrow white base; its asset is credibility with London and with African moderates who reject both Smith and armed struggle.

3.name: Cold Comfort Farm Society
3.text:
The Cold Comfort Farm Society runs a multiracial cooperative farm outside Salisbury founded in the mid-1960s. Its moving spirit is Guy Clutton-Brock, a British Christian socialist long active in African rural development, working alongside the young nationalist Didymus Mutasa. In 1970 it operates legally but under growing police suspicion.

The society preaches racial equality through shared work, cooperative ownership of land and African self-reliance. It rejects both settler rule and violent revolution, favouring a democratic, socialist path to majority rule. Its influence is moral rather than electoral: it links liberal churchmen, British sympathisers and African nationalists, and it gives the government a convenient target for accusations of subversion.

4.name: Zimbabwe African People's Union
4.text:
The Zimbabwe African People's Union was founded in 1961 by Joshua Nkomo and banned in 1962. Nkomo is held in detention at Gonakudzingwa, while James Chikerema and Jason Moyo direct the movement from exile in Lusaka. Its armed wing, ZIPRA, fought alongside the ANC's Umkhonto we Sizwe in the Wankie and Sipolilo campaigns of 1967 and 1968.

ZAPU demands immediate majority rule and the overthrow of the Smith regime. It relies on Soviet and Eastern bloc arms, training and money, and enjoys recognition from the OAU. Its base is strongest among the Ndebele and in the towns and railway centres, but the exiled leadership is increasingly divided by personal and tribal quarrels.

5.name: Zimbabwe African National Union
5.text:
The Zimbabwe African National Union broke away from ZAPU in 1963 under Ndabaningi Sithole, Herbert Chitepo and Robert Mugabe, and was banned in 1964. Sithole and Mugabe are in prison, and Sithole was sentenced in 1969 for plotting against Smith's life. In Lusaka, Chitepo chairs the external leadership and the Dare reChimurenga war council.

ZANU rejects negotiation and preaches protracted armed struggle to liberate Zimbabwe. It looks to China for weapons and training rather than to Moscow, and borrows heavily from Maoist thought. Its support lies among the Shona-speaking majority, teachers, students and migrant workers, and its exiled cadres are rethinking strategy after the costly failures of early incursions.

6.name: Masvikiro
6.text:
The masvikiro are the Shona spirit mediums who speak for the mhondoro, the ancestral guardians of the land. Ranked by the importance of the spirits they host, among them the line of Nehanda in the Zambezi valley, they command deep authority in the rural north-east. In 1970 they stand apart from both government and parties.

The mediums regard the land as belonging to the ancestors and see the Land Tenure Act and the missionary order as a desecration. They reject Western religion and settler authority alike, and recall the 1896 risings against the British. Their leverage lies in legitimacy: any movement that wins their blessing gains the trust of peasants in the remote valleys.

7.name: Central Intelligence Organisation
7.text:
The Central Intelligence Organisation was created in 1963 and is directed by Ken Flower, a former police officer. Answering directly to the Prime Minister, it runs Rhodesia's foreign intelligence, counter-insurgency networks, informers in the African townships and the covert channels that keep sanctions from biting.

The CIO serves a state that defies Britain, the Commonwealth and the United Nations, and it acts accordingly: secretive, ruthless and loyal only to the survival of the regime. It works closely with the South African and Portuguese services. Its power rests on files, informers and the trust of Ian Smith, and its assessments shape every decision on war and negotiation.

8.name: Khoja Jamaat
8.text:
The Khoja Jamaat is the small communal body of Shia traders of Gujarati origin in Salisbury and Bulawayo, many of whom came south from East Africa. Its members run shops and wholesale businesses and meet in a modest imambargah for prayer, education and Muharram gatherings.

The community favours education, commerce and quiet coexistence with whatever government rules. It keeps aloof from settler politics but resents the restrictions that racial laws place on Asian residence and trade. Its influence is limited to its own members, though its business networks reach into Malawi, Zambia and Mozambique and give it a voice in the Asian chambers of commerce.

9.name: Hussaini Majlis
9.text:
The Hussaini Majlis is a devotional assembly of young Shia men in Salisbury who gather around visiting preachers from East Africa and the Indian subcontinent. They organise the Muharram mourning rituals and read the works of clerics trained in Najaf.

Its members insist on strict religious observance and look to the senior Shia clergy rather than to community elders for guidance. They see the settler state as an alien Christian order and the West as morally corrupt, though they lack any political organisation. Their significance lies only in the future: a seedbed of religious activism should the wider Shia world turn revolutionary.

10.name: Tablighi Jamaat
10.text:
The Tablighi Jamaat, the missionary movement founded in India in 1926, reached southern Africa through the Gujarati Muslim communities in the 1960s. In Rhodesia its preaching parties travel between the mosques of Salisbury, Bulawayo and Gwelo, and among Malawian Muslim labourers on the farms and mines.

The movement shuns politics entirely and calls Muslims back to prayer, piety and correct personal conduct. It accepts the existing authorities, avoids confrontation with the settler state and teaches obedience. Its influence rests on a dense network of mosques, traders and itinerant preachers, which gives it more reach among Rhodesia's small Muslim population than any other body.

11.name: Dar al-Hijra
11.text:
Dar al-Hijra is a tiny circle of young Muslims in Salisbury, mostly sons of traders who studied in Pakistan, Egypt or Saudi Arabia. They return with pamphlets on the caliphate and a conviction that Muslims in a land ruled by unbelievers must eventually emigrate or resist.

The circle rejects both the settler republic and the African nationalists as secular, and dreams of a single Islamic state uniting the Muslim world. It condemns the West and the Soviet Union alike. Its members number a few dozen, have no arms and no following beyond their study sessions, and are known to the Special Branch mainly as a curiosity.

12.name: Ummah Study Circle
12.text:
The Ummah Study Circle brings together educated Muslims in Salisbury and Bulawayo, teachers, clerks and professionals of Asian and Malawian origin, who read the works of Hasan al-Banna and Abul A'la Maududi. It meets in private homes and mosque rooms and corresponds with Muslim youth groups in South Africa.

The circle wants Muslims to engage in public life, build schools and welfare bodies, and press for equal rights for Asians and Africans. It condemns racial discrimination as contrary to Islam but avoids open defiance of the regime. Its influence is small, resting on education and social work, but it offers a bridge between Islam and the wider struggle for civil rights.

13.name: Government House
13.text:
Government House in Salisbury is the seat of Clifford Dupont, appointed Officer Administering the Government after UDI in place of the Queen's governor. Since Sir Humphrey Gibbs resigned in 1969, Dupont is the sole head of state the regime recognises, and he is expected to become president once the republic is proclaimed.

Around him gathers the senior civil service, the judiciary and the permanent secretaries who keep an unrecognised state functioning. They value order, legality and continuity above party politics and resent both British pressure and right-wing adventurism. Their leverage lies in administering the machinery of government, signing emergency regulations and lending the rebellion a constitutional face.

14.name: Council of Chiefs
14.text:
The Council of Chiefs gathers the government-recognised chiefs of the Shona and Ndebele, who administer the Tribal Trust Lands under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In 1964 an indaba of chiefs endorsed independence on the regime's terms, and the 1969 constitution grants them ten seats in the new Senate.

The chiefs defend customary law, their control over land allocation and their salaries from the state. They distrust the nationalist parties, which denounce them as government puppets, yet they also resent land seizures and forced destocking. Their leverage lies in their authority over rural Africans and in the regime's need for African voices to claim it has popular consent.

15.name: Rhodesia National Farmers' Union
15.text:
The Rhodesia National Farmers' Union, founded in 1942, represents the white commercial farmers who hold most of the country's best land. Tobacco growers once dominated it, but sanctions have closed their markets and forced a hurried shift to maize, cotton, beef and wheat.

The union lobbies for subsidies, guaranteed prices and labour supply, and it guards the Land Tenure Act that reserves half the country for whites. It supports the Rhodesian Front but grumbles at the costs of UDI and quietly welcomes any settlement that would reopen export markets. Its leverage lies in rural constituencies, foreign-exchange earnings and the regime's dependence on agriculture to survive sanctions.

16.name: Associated Chambers of Commerce of Rhodesia
16.english: Associated Chambers of Commerce of Rhodesia
16.text:
The Associated Chambers of Commerce of Rhodesia unites the merchants, importers and retailers of Salisbury, Bulawayo and the smaller towns. Many of its members opposed UDI in 1965, fearing exactly the sanctions, controls and shortages that now shape their daily business.

The chambers argue for free trade, low taxes and the dismantling of import quotas and exchange controls. They favour a settlement with Britain and an orderly opening of the economy, though most members accept the regime as a fact of life. Their influence lies in their expertise in sanctions-busting trade routes through South Africa and Mozambique, which makes the government reliant on them even as it ignores their politics.

17.name: Natural Resources Board
17.text:
The Natural Resources Board was established in 1941 to halt soil erosion, deforestation and the destruction of watersheds. It works through intensive conservation area committees of farmers and officials and campaigns on behalf of the national parks, from Wankie to the Zambezi valley.

The board preaches careful land husbandry, contour ridging, controlled grazing and wildlife protection. Its policies have also justified the forced destocking and land rules that anger African peasants in the Tribal Trust Lands. It stands outside party politics, drawing on white farmers, wildlife rangers and scientists, and its leverage lies in statutory powers over land use and the prestige of conservation.

18.name: Railway African Workers' Union
18.text:
The Railway African Workers' Union is one of the oldest African unions in Rhodesia, organising the workers of Rhodesia Railways in Bulawayo and along the lines. Joshua Nkomo served as its organising secretary in the 1950s, and it remains a cradle of nationalist leaders. Under the emergency laws it survives only by avoiding open politics.

The union fights for wages, housing and the end of the industrial colour bar that reserves skilled jobs for whites. Its members want majority rule but prefer strikes and bargaining to guerrilla war. Its leverage lies in the railways, the artery that carries Rhodesia's sanctions-busting trade south to South Africa and east to the Mozambican ports.

19.name: Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army
19.text:
The Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army is the armed wing of ZANU, formed in the mid-1960s and led from Lusaka by the party's war council under Herbert Chitepo. Its cadres, trained in China, Tanzania and Ghana, fought the first skirmish of the war at Sinoia in 1966 and suffered heavy losses.

ZANLA is now studying the lessons of Mao's people's war: politicise the peasants first, operate in small groups and avoid head-on clashes with Rhodesian forces. It aims to infiltrate the north-east through Mozambique alongside FRELIMO. Its strength lies in Chinese instructors and a growing pool of recruits, and its success will depend on winning the rural masses.

20.name: Kith and Kin
20.text:
Kith and Kin is the populist settler right on the Rhodesian Front backbenches and in the party branches, taking its name from the appeal to British sympathy for their blood relatives in Africa. Its best-known figure is Lord Graham, a former minister and one of the signatories of UDI.

It demands complete separate development on the South African model, a halt to African advancement and no compromise whatsoever with Britain. It distrusts the urban establishment and accuses Smith of softness whenever he talks to London. Its base is white artisans, small farmers and recent immigrants, and its leverage lies in pressure on the RF caucus and the threat of a right-wing split.

21.name: Iron Laager
21.text:
Iron Laager is a loose network of militant whites in police reserve units, rifle clubs and rural farm-security associations who believe Rhodesia must be defended by force alone. Some admire the Afrikaner far right and the radical anti-communist literature arriving from Britain and the United States.

They want a strictly segregated white state, harsher punishment of nationalists, expulsion of liberal clergy and unlimited powers for the security forces. They despise parliament as weak and see Smith's ministers as too willing to bargain. Few in number, they matter through their weapons and their presence in the reserves, and through the fear that they could take matters into their own hands.

22.name: Rhodesian Security Forces
22.text:
The Rhodesian Security Forces comprise the Rhodesian Army under Lieutenant-General Keith Coster, the Royal Rhodesian Air Force and the British South Africa Police. Their elite units include the Rhodesian Light Infantry, the Special Air Service and the Rhodesian African Rifles, whose black soldiers are led by white officers.

The forces have stayed loyal to the regime since UDI and have defeated every guerrilla incursion from Zambia so far, often with South African police support. The officer corps is professional, conservative and anti-communist, and it values efficiency over politics. Its leverage is decisive: no Rhodesian government can survive without the army, and no settlement can stand against its opposition.

23.name: House of Khumalo
23.text:
The House of Khumalo is the royal lineage of Mzilikazi and Lobengula, kings of the Ndebele, whose state at Bulawayo was destroyed by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company in 1893. Lobengula's descendants live on without crown or recognition, while the Ndebele remain a proud minority in Matabeleland.

Royalists dream of restoring the Ndebele monarchy and of regaining the land taken by the settlers. They distrust both the settler state and the Shona-dominated nationalist movements, though many back ZAPU. Their leverage is cultural and historical: the memory of the kingdom still binds Ndebele identity, and any power that seeks Matabeleland's loyalty must reckon with it.
